lessons.title: Case Study: Tracing One Indian SME's Tax Year From Profit to Paid

body.text: Every rule in this course belongs to one company, in one year, on one set of dates. This lesson follows a single business from its audited profit to the money that actually leaves its bank account, and then counts what carelessness cost it.

children.text: Meenakshi Components Private Limited makes pump parts in Coimbatore. Turnover is about ₹18 crore, it employs 64 people, and it has been in the concessional regime under section 200 [old 115BAA] for three years. Its audited profit before tax for the year is ₹1,40,00,000. Nothing about it is unusual, which is the point.

body.title: One tax year, start to finish

events.title: The year opens
events.description: Books open, the finance executive builds a profit forecast, and the first advance tax estimate is prepared from it rather than from last year's figure.

events.title: Advance tax instalments
events.description: 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% cumulative under section 408 [old 211]. The company estimated ₹30,00,000 of tax for the year and paid to that schedule.

events.title: TDS and GST
events.description: TDS deducted and deposited by the 7th, GSTR-1 by the 11th and GSTR-3B by the 20th, with GSTR-2B reconciled before any credit was claimed.

events.title: Year-end housekeeping
events.description: Statutory dues cleared, and unpaid micro and small supplier bills reviewed against the 45-day rule in section 37(2)(g) [old 43B(h)].

events.title: Form No. 26
events.description: The tax audit report under section 63 [old 44AB] is filed one month before the return.

events.title: Return filed
events.description: Filed under section 263(1) [old 139(1)] with a digital signature, and the balance tax paid as self-assessment tax.

body.title: Try It: Check the Tax
body.prompt: Taxable income is ₹1,37,00,000 and the company is in the concessional regime, taxed at an effective 25.168%. What is the tax for the year? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: ₹1,37,00,000 × 25.168% is ₹34,48,016, or about ₹34.48 lakh. Note that this is 24.63% of the ₹1,40,00,000 book profit, because taxable income came out lower than book profit this year. Next year, when the ₹2,80,000 of supplier dues and the ₹90,000 disallowance reverse, the relationship will move the other way.

children.text: Step Two: What the Timing Cost

The company estimated ₹30,00,000 of tax in April and paid to that schedule all year: ₹4,50,000 by June, ₹13,50,000 by September, ₹22,50,000 by December and ₹30,00,000 by March. The final figure turned out to be ₹34,48,016. That gap has two separate consequences.

cells: Covered by the relief for the first instalment
Covered by the relief for the second instalment

children.text: The June and September instalments escaped interest because the law gives limited relief where a company has paid above a specified proportion of its final liability by those two dates. The December and March instalments get no such relief, so 3% and 1% apply to the shortfalls.

Then section 424 [old 234B] applies separately, because the ₹30,00,000 paid during the year is below 90% of the final ₹34,48,016, which is ₹31,03,214. Interest runs at 1% a month on the unpaid ₹4,48,016 from the start of the next tax year until the balance is paid with the return in October, which is seven months, or ₹31,361.
Total interest is ₹45,921. Paying an extra ₹1,03,214 by 31 March would have cleared the 90% test and removed ₹31,361 of it, and a proper December re-estimate would have removed most of the rest.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Interest Was Avoidable at Year End?
body.question: On 25 March, the finance executive realises the final tax will be about ₹34,48,016 rather than ₹30,00,000. What could she still have done on that date?
options: Nothing. Both interest charges were already fixed by 15 March
Paid an extra ₹1,03,214 before 31 March to cross the 90% test and avoid the section 424 [old 234B] interest
Paid the full balance to avoid all interest, including section 425 [old 234C]
Filed the return early in April to stop the interest running
body.explanation: Tax paid up to 31 March still counts as advance tax for the year, so crossing 90% of the final liability by then would have kept section 424 away entirely. The section 425 interest on the December and March instalments was already fixed and could not be undone. Filing early does not help either, because section 424 interest runs from the start of the next tax year regardless of when the return goes in.

children.text: Nothing in this company's year was aggressive, disputed or even interesting. It simply leaked. Here is the same year, priced item by item.

body.label: The cost of an ordinary, careless year
body.context: Permanently lost on a ₹1,40,00,000 profit, with no dispute, no notice and no clever planning involved. That is roughly 1.2% of profit before tax, or about 4.8% of the year's tax bill.

body.text: Notice what is not on that list. No aggressive structure, no GAAR question, no scrutiny assessment. The money went on a donation booked in the wrong place, a few cash payments, one missed TDS check, a supplier paid late, a GST return filed late, and an advance tax estimate nobody revisited in December. Every one of those is a process fix, not a tax strategy.

children.text: Step Four: Getting the Money to the Owner

The founder draws a salary of ₹24,00,000, which sits inside the ₹1,40,00,000 profit figure as an expense and has already reduced the company's tax. After the year end, the board declares a dividend of ₹20,00,000 out of post-tax profits. The company deducts 10% TDS under section 393 [old 194], and the founder adds the gross dividend to her own income, where it is taxed at her slab rate, with the TDS available as credit.

columns.label: What actually happened
points: Advance tax estimated once in April and never revised
TDS checked at audit time, not at invoice entry
Supplier payment terms uniform at 60 days, regardless of who the supplier was
A donation booked as a business expense
One GST return filed late, with the penalty also disallowed

columns.label: What next year looks like
points: A fresh estimate ten days before each of the four instalment dates
TDS validated when the invoice is entered, with a running annual total per vendor
Micro and small suppliers tagged and paid within 45 days
Donations made personally or with the regime consequence understood in advance
GST calendar owned by a named person, with the portal checked monthly

body.title: Scenario: The Board Meeting After the Return Is Filed
body.scenario: The return has been filed in October. The founder asks three questions at the board meeting. Why is our tax rate 24.63% when everyone says 25.17%? Should we buy the second machine we need in March or wait for April? And should we look again at whether the old regime with its incentives would suit us better now that we are investing heavily?
body.prompt: Answer all three, using what this course has covered.
body.modelAnswer: On the first, 24.63% is the tax measured against book profit, while 25.168% is the rate applied to taxable income, and this year taxable income was ₹3,00,000 lower than book profit because tax depreciation of ₹35,00,000 outran the ₹32,00,000 of add-backs. It is not a discount, and it will reverse: when the supplier dues and the TDS disallowance are settled, and as depreciation on existing blocks tapers, the effective rate will drift above the headline. On the second, a machine put to use in March earns only half the depreciation rate for that year, while one commissioned in April earns the full rate in the next year and carries a higher written down value forward. On tax alone, April wins. But if the machine would earn revenue through March, or if capacity is constraining an order, the commercial gain will usually dwarf the tax difference, so the right question is when the machine can start earning, not which year it lands in. On the third, the old regime only wins if incentive deductions exceed roughly 28% of taxable income for a company at the 30% base rate, and around 13.6% at 25%. This company has no SEZ unit and no research incentives, and the additional depreciation it would gain access to is a timing benefit rather than a permanent one. Staying in the old regime would also bring it inside minimum alternate tax at 14% of book profit, which since the Finance Act, 2026 is a final tax with no credit. And in any case the section 200 option is irrevocable, so the company cannot go back. The honest answer to the third question is that the regime is settled and the real gains now are the ₹1,66,728 of leaks, not a structural change.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Test Worth Remembering
body.textWithBlank: Paying at least ___ percent of your final tax liability as advance tax by 31 March keeps section 424 [old 234B] interest away entirely.
body.explanation: Ninety percent. For this company the gap was ₹1,03,214, and closing it on 30 March would have saved ₹31,361 of interest. It is the highest-return ten minutes of work in the entire tax calendar.

body.title: The Whole Course, as One Annual Routine
steps: April: confirm your regime, build a profit forecast, and set the year's compliance calendar with named owners
Monthly: deduct TDS at invoice entry, deposit by the 7th, file GSTR-1 by the 11th and GSTR-3B by the 20th after reconciling GSTR-2B
Before each advance tax date: re-estimate the full year from actuals, apply your effective rate, and pay the cumulative target
Quarterly: review disallowance-prone spending, cash payments, related party payments and personal expenses
February: review unpaid micro and small supplier dues and clear anything past the deadline
March: settle statutory dues, check the 90% advance tax test, and decide asset purchases on commercial grounds with the 180-day rule in mind
September: file Form No. 26, having given the auditor the fixed asset register and TDS reconciliation early
October: file the return with a valid digital signature, then watch the portal for the intimation
Every year: re-read the Budget changes, because rates, thresholds and even section numbers move

cards.definition: The 22% concessional regime, effective 25.168%, irrevocable, and outside minimum alternate tax.
The bridge from audited book profit to taxable income, through add-backs and tax depreciation.
Depreciation on blocks of assets at prescribed rates, with half rates for assets used under 180 days in the first year.
Deductions allowed only on actual payment, including dues to micro and small suppliers under 37(2)(g).
Carry forward of business losses for eight years, preserved only by filing the return on time.
Interest for paying advance tax short, and for deferring instalments through the year.
TDS on salary, TDS on everything else, and TCS, replacing the old 194 series and section 206C.
Tax audit, reported in Form No. 26 one month before the return.
GST on purchases, claimable only when the invoice appears in your GSTR-2B and the supplier has paid.
The single twelve-month concept in the Income-tax Act, 2025, replacing previous year and assessment year.

points: A real tax year runs from an audited profit through a computation, four advance tax dates, twelve months of TDS and GST, an audit report and a return
This company's ₹1,40,00,000 of book profit became ₹1,37,00,000 of taxable income and ₹34,48,016 of tax, an effective 24.63% on book profit
Careless timing added ₹45,921 of non-deductible interest that a December re-estimate and a March top-up would have removed
Ordinary slips cost ₹2,59,849 in total, of which ₹1,66,728 is permanently gone
None of the losses came from aggressive positions or disputes. They came from process
Tax management in a small business is mostly a calendar, a few checks at invoice entry, and one honest re-estimate every quarter
Rates, thresholds and section numbers change every year, so the routine matters more than any single number in this course

body.text: This case study is illustrative and for educational purposes only. Meenakshi Components Private Limited is fictional, and the figures are constructed to demonstrate the provisions covered in this course rather than to model any real business. Nothing here constitutes tax, legal or investment advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets, and rates and thresholds change with each Union Budget. Work through your own numbers with a qualified chartered accountant.
